— Conflicting opinions and research outcomes

Evidence clusters show two opposing positions: multiple sources report broad-spectrum pesticides harm many insect groups and other wildlife [d1][d3][d4][d6][d8], while other sources argue certain pesticides or application methods can be selective and less harmful to beneficial insects [d5][d7][d9]. This constitutes mutually incompatible claims within the same scope.

Pesticides are widely reported to harm a broad range of insects and other wildlife beyond bees, including butterflies, beetles, and soil invertebrates, with independent reviews describing broad-spectrum chemicals as indiscriminate in their effects [d1][d3][d4][d8]. Some research, however, indicates that certain pesticides or application methods can be more targeted, with insecticidal soaps and properly used neonicotinoids showing less impact on beneficial insects [d5][d7]. Farmers also report efforts to avoid harming beneficial insects due to economic concerns, suggesting variability in harm depending on practices [d9]. Overall, evidence supports both that pesticides can be harmful to many insects and that not all pesticides harm all insects uniformly [d2][d6].
